implementation_notes: On Android the OS-managed store replaces the channel: WorkManager keeps scheduled work in its own SQLite database and reschedules it across process death and device reboots, so enqueueing a unique work request is 'accepted durably' and the worker returning Result.retry() is the redelivery loop with a configured backoff. The classic structure survives only as the worker's contract: a stable business id in inputData (not a fresh id per attempt) plus idempotent work, because the system may re-run a worker it is unsure about; payloads larger than the inputData limit must be persisted elsewhere and referenced. For JVM backends the equivalent store is a broker transaction (next variant).
pitfalls: WorkManager may run a worker more than once (it cannot always tell whether a killed run completed), so the worker must be idempotent and use a stable business id rather than a fresh uuid.
ExistingWorkPolicy and the backoff criteria must be chosen deliberately: KEEP silently drops a re-scheduled delivery, REPLACE cancels one already in flight.
inputData is capped (about 10 KB): large payloads belong in the database or a file with a reference in the work request.
WorkManager's database is not the app's database: enqueueing inside an app transaction is still a dual write unless both live in one Room database.

variants.name: JVM Kafka transactional producer wrapped in coroutines
variants.idiom_name: KafkaProducer transactions on Dispatchers.IO with use {}
variants.implementation_notes: Backend Kotlin uses the JVM Kafka client, so the guarantee is the broker's: idempotence for retry-safety and a transaction (initTransactions, beginTransaction, commitTransaction, sendOffsetsToTransaction) to commit output and consumer offset together. Kotlin adds only the wrapper: the blocking producer must run on Dispatchers.IO (or a dedicated dispatcher), the producer is closed with use {} so buffered records are flushed, and suspending call sites keep the ack path in one coroutine scope. The classic per-hop store remains the broker log; no Kotlin-specific durability primitive exists.
pitfalls: KafkaProducer is thread-safe but has no coroutine awareness: every blocking call must be on Dispatchers.IO, or the whole dispatcher stalls.
Skipping initTransactions() makes the first beginTransaction fail, and an abandoned transaction blocks the transactional id until its timeout.
Closing the producer without flushing (use {} does flush, a leaked instance does not) drops buffered records.
A transactional id that is regenerated per process start loses zombie fencing; it must be stable and owned by one instance.
